beats.narration: Begin by framing Course Foundations and Scope as a question about inputs, decisions, and observable results. This course offers an introduction to supervised machine learning theories and algorithms, and their application to classification and regression tasks. Consider this worked case: Students will implement a basic classification model using scikit-learn to predict customer churn from tabular data. On screen, display a slide showing the course title, duration (8-12 min), and a simple flowchart linking 'Supervised Learning' to 'Classification/Regression' with a note about programming assignments. List the givens before choosing a method, because an unstated assumption can change the conclusion. This establishes the vocabulary and scope needed for the remaining sections.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a slide showing the course title, duration (8-12 min), and a simple flowchart linking 'Supervised Learning' to 'Classification/Regression' with a note about programming assignments.

beats.narration: Now define Mathematical Background and Data Visualization precisely enough that another learner could test the definition. Topics include: Mathematical background of machine learning (for example statistical analysis and visualization of data), neural models (for example Convolutional Neural Networks, Recurrent Neural Networks), probabilistic graphical models (for example Bayesian networks, Markov models), and reinforcement learning. Consider this worked case: Students will plot a histogram and scatter plot of training data to identify outliers and feature correlations before model training. On screen, show a split-screen image: left side shows a histogram of a continuous feature, right side shows a scatter plot of two features, with axes labeled and a legend indicating 'Training Data Distribution'. Separate the formal definition from an implementation detail, then identify what evidence would distinguish them. A precise definition makes later examples easier to evaluate and revise.
beats.title: Mathematical Background and Data Visualization
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a split-screen image: left side shows a histogram of a continuous feature, right side shows a scatter plot of two features, with axes labeled and a legend indicating 'Training Data Distribution'.

beats.narration: With the foundation in place, examine how Machine Learning Workflows and Data Preparation operates in a concrete sequence. Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Consider this worked case: Students will use a scikit-learn Pipeline to standardize features and train a logistic regression model without mixing preprocessing steps across splits. On screen, display a horizontal timeline graphic with six labeled nodes: 'Data Preparation', 'Training', 'Validation', 'Testing', 'Model Selection', 'Evaluation', connected by arrows indicating sequential execution. Follow every arrow in order and name the state before and after each transition. The trace converts an abstract statement into an inspectable sequence.
beats.title: Machine Learning Workflows and Data Preparation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a horizontal timeline graphic with six labeled nodes: 'Data Preparation', 'Training', 'Validation', 'Testing', 'Model Selection', 'Evaluation', connected by arrows indicating sequential execution.

beats.narration: Next, compare the choices involved in Preventing Data Leakage and Cross-Validation and make the decision criteria explicit. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Consider this worked case: Students will implement StratifiedKFold cross-validation to evaluate a random forest classifier, ensuring scaling is applied only within each fold's training set. On screen, show a diagram of a dataset split into 5 folds, with one fold highlighted as 'Validation' and the others as 'Training', accompanied by a warning icon labeled 'No Leakage'. Compare alternatives against the same constraints so the evaluation does not move the goalposts. Using shared criteria turns a preference into a defensible technical choice.
beats.title: Preventing Data Leakage and Cross-Validation
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a diagram of a dataset split into 5 folds, with one fold highlighted as 'Validation' and the others as 'Training', accompanied by a warning icon labeled 'No Leakage'.

beats.narration: Apply Evaluation Metrics and Error Costs to a worked situation instead of treating it as an isolated definition. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Consider this worked case: Students will compare precision, recall, and F1-score for a medical diagnosis classifier, weighting recall higher due to the high cost of false negatives. On screen, display a comparison table with columns for 'Metric', 'Definition', and 'Use Case', highlighting 'Recall' under 'High Cost of False Negatives' with a red alert icon. Work from the concrete inputs to the result, checking units, types, or invariants at each step. The worked case shows both how to apply the method and how to check it.
beats.title: Evaluation Metrics and Error Costs
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a comparison table with columns for 'Metric', 'Definition', and 'Use Case', highlighting 'Recall' under 'High Cost of False Negatives' with a red alert icon.

beats.narration: Examine the tradeoffs in Neural Models: CNNs and RNNs, including what improves and what becomes more difficult. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. Consider this worked case: Students will train a CNN on a dataset of handwritten digits to classify images, and an RNN on a time-series dataset to predict stock prices. On screen, show two side-by-side architecture diagrams: left shows a CNN with convolutional and pooling layers processing an image, right shows an RNN with hidden states processing a sequence of data points. State the benefit, the cost, and the condition under which the tradeoff is acceptable. Making the tradeoff visible prevents a local improvement from hiding a larger cost.
beats.title: Neural Models: CNNs and RNNs
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show two side-by-side architecture diagrams: left shows a CNN with convolutional and pooling layers processing an image, right shows an RNN with hidden states processing a sequence of data points.

beats.narration: Stress-test the reasoning around Probabilistic Graphical Models with an edge case and identify which assumption controls the outcome. Programming assignments are required. Consider this worked case: Students will construct a Bayesian network to model the probability of disease given symptoms, using conditional probability tables for each node. On screen, display a directed acyclic graph with nodes labeled 'Symptom A', 'Symptom B', and 'Disease', connected by arrows indicating causal relationships, with probability values annotated on edges. Change one assumption at a time and observe which part of the reasoning no longer holds. The edge case reveals the boundary of the claim without discarding the useful core idea.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a directed acyclic graph with nodes labeled 'Symptom A', 'Symptom B', and 'Disease', connected by arrows indicating causal relationships, with probability values annotated on edges.

beats.narration: Use Reinforcement Learning Basics to diagnose a failure by separating symptoms, causes, and corrective action. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Consider this worked case: Students will train an agent to navigate a grid environment using Q-learning, adjusting actions based on cumulative reward signals. On screen, show a simple grid environment with an agent icon, arrows indicating possible actions, and a reward value (+1 or -1) displayed at each step, with a 'Policy' label indicating the learned strategy. Locate the first point where observed behavior diverges from expected behavior, then test the smallest plausible cause. The diagnosis is strongest when another person can reproduce the observation and the test.
beats.title: Reinforcement Learning Basics
beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Show a simple grid environment with an agent icon, arrows indicating possible actions, and a reward value (+1 or -1) displayed at each step, with a 'Policy' label indicating the learned strategy.

beats.narration: Connect NIST AI Risk Management Framework to the earlier ideas and explain how the pieces work as one system. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Consider this worked case: Students will document a risk map for a deployed recommendation system, identifying potential biases in training data and outlining monitoring procedures for post-deployment performance. On screen, display a four-quadrant diagram labeled 'Govern', 'Map', 'Measure', 'Manage', with each quadrant containing a brief description and a relevant icon (e.g., shield for security, magnifying glass for measurement). Explain each connection explicitly and verify that information retains the same meaning across representations. The synthesis matters only if every connection remains supported by the original evidence.

beats.visualDirection: template:academic-process | Display a four-quadrant diagram labeled 'Govern', 'Map', 'Measure', 'Manage', with each quadrant containing a brief description and a relevant icon (e.g., shield for security, magnifying glass for measurement).

beats.narration: Finish with Practical Analysis Checklist as a practical checklist that can guide a new analysis. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results. Consider this worked case: Students will complete a checklist verifying that preprocessing was fitted only on training data, cross-validation was used, evaluation metrics matched the task, and monitoring plans are in place. On screen, create an editable process diagram for Practical Analysis Checklist with labeled inputs, decisions, state changes, and a checked output. For each checklist item, record the evidence, the remaining uncertainty, and the next verification step. The result is a repeatable procedure, not a conclusion that depends on memory or intuition.

sources.author: scikit-learn developers
sources.excerpt: Machine-learning workflows separate data preparation, training, validation, testing, model selection, and evaluation. Supervised methods learn a mapping from examples paired with target labels. Unsupervised methods identify structure without target labels. Preprocessing must be fitted only on permitted training data to avoid leakage. Pipelines combine preprocessing and estimators so the same transformations are applied consistently. Cross-validation repeats training and validation across defined data splits. Evaluation metrics must match the task and the cost of different errors. Hyperparameter selection must remain separate from final test evaluation. Leakage, distribution shift, overfitting, and unexamined assumptions can invalidate results.

sources.author: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.excerpt: The NIST AI Risk Management Framework organizes work around Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage. Govern establishes policies, responsibilities, and accountability for AI risk. Map documents context, intended use, affected people, and potential impacts. Measure uses qualitative and quantitative methods to analyze identified risks. Manage prioritizes risks and allocates resources for response and monitoring. Risk analysis considers data quality and uncertainty. It also considers robustness, privacy, security, transparency, and fairness. Monitoring continues after deployment because context and system behavior can change.
